subject: Mathematics
board: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9–1) Mathematics (1MA1), Higher tier
source: Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 specification as recorded in content/syllabus/ks4/mathematics.json (units N and A only), Higher tier with Foundation-accessible starts; Edexcel 1MA1 Higher exam style; INSET lesson standard. Skipped as already taught well in the school's existing mathematics lessons: N4 primes/HCF/LCM, N7 fractional and negative indices, N8 surds, N10 recurring decimals (existing Year 10 lessons 1-5); A4 binomials and quadratic factorising, A5 subject appearing twice, A6 identities and proof, A17 linear equations, A21 forming equations, A22 linear inequalities (existing Year 10 lessons 6-16); A11/A12 quadratic, cubic and reciprocal graphs, A13 translations and reflections of graphs, A17 solving by graphs, A19 algebraic simultaneous equations (existing Year 11 lessons 1-8).

lessons.title: Units and compound measures
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does the unit matter as much as the number?
objectives: Convert between metric units of length, area, volume, mass and time
Use compound measures: speed, density and pressure
Convert compound units such as km/h to m/s
successCriteria: All: convert simple metric units
Most: convert area and volume units and use speed, density and pressure formulae
Some: convert compound units and solve multi-step problems
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: density, pressure and speed; Geography: map and journey data
lessons.smsc: Moral: accuracy and honest units in measurement and trade

keywords.def: a measure made from two units, such as speed in km/h
mass ÷ volume
force ÷ area
distance ÷ time

teach.heading: Metric conversions
bullets: Area units multiply the length factor twice
teach.note: Draw a 1 m square split into 100 cm by 100 cm. 3.5 m² = 35 000 cm².

teach.heading: Speed, density, pressure
bullets: Density = mass ÷ volume: 540 g in 200 cm³ is 2.7 g/cm³
Pressure = force ÷ area: 600 N on 0.3 m² is 2000 N/m²
Average speed uses total distance ÷ total time
teach.note: Use a triangle diagram for rearranging. 150 km in 2 h 30 min: 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h; write 2 h 30 as 2.5, not 2.3.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Area and volume conversions do not use the length factor once
teach.note: Compare 100 and 10 000.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.why: 5 × 10 000 = 50 000. A uses the length factor once.

practice: Convert 3.5 m² to cm² and 2.4 litres to cm³
A car travels 150 km in 2 h 30. Find its average speed.
A block has mass 540 g and volume 200 cm³. Find its density.
Convert 1.2 g/cm³ to kg/m³.
independent: Core: (a) 4500 g in kg (b) 2 h 15 min in hours (c) speed of 90 km in 1.5 h
Extend: A force of 600 N acts on an area of 0.3 m². Find the pressure. Convert 20 m/s to km/h.
Stretch: A solid has density 8.5 g/cm³ and mass 2.38 kg. Find its volume in cm³ and in m³.
exit: Convert 2 m² to cm²
Speed for 45 km in 30 minutes, in km/h
Density of 90 g in 36 cm³
lessons.homework: Eight conversion and compound-measure questions from science and geography contexts.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: formula triangles; unit-conversion table. Stretch: unit conversions with density in kg/m³.

lessons.title: Estimating and checking calculations
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you know a calculator answer is sensible before you trust it?
objectives: Estimate answers by rounding to 1 significant figure
Decide whether an estimate is an over- or under-estimate
Check calculations using inverse operations and technology sensibly
successCriteria: All: estimate by rounding to 1 s.f.
Most: estimate with fractions and roots and say if it is an over-estimate or under-estimate
Some: detect calculator slips from an estimate
lessons.smsc: Moral: taking responsibility to check one's own work before relying on it

keywords.def: an approximate answer from simple numbers
a digit counted from the first non-zero digit
bigger than the true value
undo the calculation to check it

teach.heading: Round, then calculate
teach.note: Show an inverse check: 94.56 ÷ 4.8 = 19.7.

model.problem: Estimate (6.12 × 31.8) ÷ 0.49 and say if it is an over- or under-estimate
steps: Numerator rounded down, denominator rounded up
So the estimate is an under-estimate (true value 397.2)

teach.heading: Rounding direction
bullets: Rounding the numerator down makes the fraction smaller
Rounding the denominator up makes the fraction smaller
Mixed changes: the effect may be unclear
teach.note: Ask pupils to predict before calculating.

teach.heading: Catching mistakes
bullets: A display of 18 is a warning: (3.2 + 4) × 2.5 was entered
teach.note: Typical errors: missing brackets, wrong key, wrong power of ten.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Do not round to 1 s.f. in the final answer unless asked
teach.note: Estimates are not answers.

misconception.right: 0.05 × 30 = 1.5; the decimal point is easy to lose

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: Which is the best estimate for 49.6 × 2.1 ÷ 0.52?
check.why: Round to 50, 2 and 0.5: 100 ÷ 0.5 = 200. B changes 0.5 into 5.

practice: Estimate 19.7 × 4.8
Estimate (6.12 × 31.8) ÷ 0.49 and say if it is over or under
Estimate √(40.3 + 8.9)
A calculator shows 3.8 × 5.2 = 19.76. Check using an estimate.
independent: Extend: Estimate (8.7 + 12.4) ÷ 0.46 and decide if it is an over- or under-estimate. Estimate √(63 × 4.1).
Stretch: A pupil says 5 + 3 ÷ 0.5 = 16. Decide if this is right and say what error was made.
exit: Estimate 38.2 × 0.92
Estimate 401 ÷ 7.9
Is 5 × 10 an over- or under-estimate of 4.8 × 9.7?
lessons.homework: Eight estimation questions and two 'is the calculator answer sensible?' tasks.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: rounding to 1 s.f. flow chart. Stretch: effects of rounding on products and quotients.

lessons.title: Rounding, significant figures and error intervals
lessons.bigQuestion: If a length is given as 3.4 cm, what could the real length be?
objectives: Round to decimal places and significant figures
Write error intervals using inequality notation
Understand truncation and rounding in context
successCriteria: All: round to d.p. and s.f.
Most: write error intervals for rounded values
Some: write error intervals for truncated values and for s.f. rounding of large numbers
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: reporting measurements; Computing: truncation in integer division
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty about the accuracy of a measurement

keywords.def: digits after the decimal point
digits counted from the first non-zero digit
range of values that round or truncate to a given number
cut off digits without rounding

teach.heading: Rounding rules
bullets: Look at the next digit: 5 or more rounds up
s.f.: start at the first non-zero digit
teach.note: Include placeholder zeros.

teach.heading: Error intervals
bullets: Lower bound included, upper bound not included
teach.note: Use a number line with half the rounding unit either side.

model.problem: A length is 520 cm to 2 significant figures. Write the error interval.

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: 525 would round up to 530.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: x = 4000 to 1 significant figure. The error interval is:
check.why: The rounding unit is 1000; half is 500. A uses the 2 s.f. interval.

practice: Round 0.004567 to 2 s.f. and 25 487 to 3 s.f.
Write the error interval for 3.4 to 1 d.p.
Write the error interval for 0.7 truncated to 1 d.p.
A bus holds 52 people. How many buses for 413 pupils?
independent: Core: Error intervals for (a) 8.5 to 1 d.p. (b) 60 to 1 s.f. (c) 0.35 to 2 d.p.
Extend: x rounds to 4.5 to 1 d.p.; y rounds to 4.50 to 2 d.p. Write both intervals and compare.
Stretch: 3.2 is a truncation to 1 d.p. of x. Write the error interval and a value of x for which rounding would give a different answer.
exit: Round 7.0449 to 3 s.f.
Error interval for 6.3 to 1 d.p.
Error interval for 1500 to 2 s.f.
lessons.homework: Eight rounding and error-interval questions, including two in a measurement context.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: number-line template with half-unit marks. Stretch: error intervals for s.f. with leading zeros.

lessons.title: Upper and lower bounds: measurements and calculations
lessons.bigQuestion: If every measurement is rounded, how accurate can a calculated answer be?
objectives: Find upper and lower bounds of a rounded value
Calculate bounds of sums, differences and products
Choose which bound to use in each calculation
successCriteria: All: state bounds of a rounded measurement (Higher only)
Most: find bounds for sums and products
Some: find bounds for differences and compound problems
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: tolerance in manufacturing; Science: measurement uncertainty

keywords.def: the top of the interval, just too large to round to the given number
the smallest value that rounds to the given number
upper and lower limits of a rounded value
the unit of rounding

starter: Bismillah. Write 3.4 to 1 d.p. as an error interval.

teach.heading: Bounds of one measurement
bullets: 4.5 cm to 1 d.p.: lower bound 4.45, upper bound 4.55
The upper bound is the limit of the interval
teach.note: Treat the upper bound as 12.5 even though the value is strictly below. Make a rule: half a unit each side.

teach.heading: Calculating with bounds
bullets: Maximum a + b: upper a + upper b
Maximum a − b: upper a − lower b
teach.note: Rectangle 12 cm by 8 cm to the nearest cm.

model.problem: A rectangle is 12 cm by 8 cm, both to the nearest cm. Find the bounds of the area.

teach.heading: Subtraction
teach.note: Check with the numbers: biggest difference needs the biggest a and smallest b.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: The upper bound of 4.5 to 1 d.p. is 4.55, not 4.54
teach.note: We use the boundary value.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: a = 9.4 and b = 3.2, both to 1 d.p. What is the maximum value of a − b?
check.why: 9.45 − 3.15 = 6.30. C is the minimum; A is the unrounded difference.

practice: Bounds of 4.5 cm (1 d.p.) and 12 kg (nearest kg)
Bounds of the area of a 12 cm by 8 cm rectangle, to the nearest cm
Maximum and minimum of a − b where a = 9.4 and b = 3.2
A mass is 85 g to the nearest g. State its bounds.
independent: Core: (a) bounds of 7.2 (1 d.p.) (b) bounds of 250 to 2 s.f. (c) maximum a + b where a = 5.1, b = 2.3 (1 d.p.)
Extend: A rectangle is 15.4 cm by 6.2 cm, 1 d.p. Find the bounds of its perimeter and area.
Stretch: Two planks of 2.4 m and 1.8 m (1 d.p.) are cut from one 4.5 m board (1 d.p.). Is it certain that the offcut is at least 0.2 m?
exit: Bounds of 6.8 to 1 d.p.
Upper bound of the area of a 5 cm by 9 cm rectangle, each to the nearest cm
Maximum of a − b if a = 20, b = 8 (nearest integer)
lessons.homework: Six bounds questions: single measurements, a product and a difference, with a clear 'use upper / use lower' annotation.
lessons.send: Higher only. SEND/EAL: table recording 'use upper' or 'use lower' for each operation. Stretch: bounds of expressions with several operations.

lessons.title: Bounds: division, formulae and sensible accuracy
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we decide how many figures to give in a final answer?
objectives: Find bounds for quotients and formulae
Use bounds in speed and density problems
Decide the accuracy to which an answer can be given
successCriteria: All: find bounds of a quotient (Higher only)
Most: apply bounds to speed and density formulae
Some: decide the sensible accuracy so that both bounds agree
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: precision of measurements in practical work
lessons.smsc: Moral: not claiming more accuracy than the data supports

keywords.def: the top of an interval
the bottom of an interval
the result of a division
how many significant figures an answer can honestly have

starter: Write bounds of 240 to the nearest 10.
Write bounds of 3 to the nearest whole.

teach.heading: Dividing
bullets: Maximum a ÷ b: upper a ÷ lower b
Minimum a ÷ b: lower a ÷ upper b
The biggest quotient needs the biggest top and the smallest bottom
Same idea for any formula with a fraction
teach.note: Use a diagram of a fraction: the denominator reduces the value.

model.problem: A distance is 240 km (nearest 10 km) and a time is 3 hours (nearest hour). Find the bounds of the speed.

teach.heading: Sensible accuracy
bullets: Density = mass ÷ volume: 85 g and 12 cm³ (nearest)
Both round to 7 to 1 s.f., so density = 7 g/cm³ (1 s.f.)
teach.note: Explain that quoting 7.08 would claim more accuracy than the data allows.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Using the upper bound of both numbers in a quotient gives a value that is not the maximum
teach.note: Maximum needs upper top and lower bottom.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: The mass is 85 g and volume 12 cm³ (nearest whole numbers). What is the lower bound for the density?
check.why: Lower bound: lower mass ÷ upper volume. B is the lower mass with the lower volume, which is not the minimum.

practice: Speed: 240 km (nearest 10 km) in 3 hours (nearest hour). Find the greatest and least speed.
Density: 85 g and 12 cm³ (nearest whole). Bounds, and value to a suitable accuracy.
Find the upper bound of 8.4 ÷ 2.1 (1 d.p. each).
A car uses 40 litres (nearest litre) over 520 km (nearest 10 km). Greatest and least km per litre.
independent: Core: (a) upper bound of 12.5 ÷ 2.5 (1 d.p.) (b) lower bound of 150 ÷ 6 (nearest integer)
Extend: A pupil walks 1.2 km (1 d.p.) in 15 minutes (nearest minute). Bounds of speed in km/h.
Stretch: v = u + at with u = 5.0, a = 2.0, t = 3.0 (all 1 d.p.). Find bounds of v and give v to a sensible accuracy.
exit: Upper bound of 60 ÷ 4 (nearest integer)
Lower bound of 9.5 ÷ 1.5 (1 d.p. each)
A density answer has bounds 6.76 and 7.43: to how many s.f. can you quote it?
lessons.homework: Six bounds problems with a sentence stating the sensible accuracy.
lessons.send: Higher only. SEND/EAL: tick-box table for upper/lower. Stretch: formula-based bounds including squares.

lessons.unit: A13-A16 Algebra: Higher graph work and real-life graphs
lessons.title: Distance-time and velocity-time graphs
lessons.bigQuestion: What can the slope of a graph and the area under it tell you about a journey?
objectives: Read and draw distance-time graphs and find speed from the gradient
Read and draw velocity-time graphs and find acceleration from the gradient
Find distance from the area under a velocity-time graph
successCriteria: All: describe a journey from a distance-time graph
Most: find speeds and accelerations from gradients
Some: find distance from an area under a velocity-time graph made of trapeziums
lessons.smsc: Social: planning journeys with care for safe and punctual travel

keywords.def: change in the y-value ÷ change in the x-value
rate of change of velocity, in m/s²
speed in a direction against time
here, the distance travelled

starter: Bismillah. Find the gradient between (0, 0) and (2, 80).
Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 20 and 40 and height 20.
What are the units of speed?

teach.heading: Distance-time graphs
teach.note: Journey with points (0, 0), (1, 40), (1.5, 40), (3, 100), (5, 0). Speeds: 40 km/h, 0, 40 km/h, then 50 km/h back. Total distance travelled 200 km in 5 h gives an average speed of 40 km/h.

teach.heading: Velocity-time graphs
bullets: Area under the graph = distance travelled
teach.note: Points (0, 0), (10, 20), (30, 20), (40, 0): acceleration 2 m/s², then constant 20 m/s, then deceleration of 2 m/s².

model.problem: A velocity-time graph passes through (0, 0), (10, 20), (30, 20), (40, 0). Find the distance travelled.
steps: Shape is a trapezium with parallel sides 40 (base) and 20 (top)

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: A flat line on a velocity-time graph is not 'stopped'
teach.note: Flat on distance-time is stopped; flat on velocity-time is constant speed.

misconception.wrong: A horizontal line on a v-t graph means the object is stationary
misconception.right: A horizontal line on a v-t graph means constant velocity; velocity 0 means stationary

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: On a distance-time graph, which feature shows the fastest part of a journey?
check.why: Gradient is speed, so the steepest line is the fastest. D is stationary.

practice: A journey has (time h, distance km) points (0, 0), (1, 40), (1.5, 40), (3, 100), (5, 0). Describe each stage and find the speed in each.
Find the average speed over the whole journey
Find the acceleration in the first 10 seconds and the deceleration at the end
Find the total distance for the velocity-time graph (0, 0), (10, 20), (30, 20), (40, 0)
independent: Core: A cyclist goes 12 km in 45 minutes. What is her speed in km/h? Draw her graph.
Extend: A train accelerates from 0 to 30 m/s in 15 s, travels at 30 m/s for 60 s, then slows to a stop in 25 s. Draw the graph and find the distance.
Stretch: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 24 m/s in 8 s, then travels at 24 m/s for 12 s. Find the total distance and the average speed over the 20 s.
exit: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph represent?
Find the area under v-t points (0, 0), (5, 10), (15, 10).
Find the average speed: 200 km in 5 hours.
lessons.homework: Two graph-interpretation questions and one drawing task, with units written in every answer.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: annotated graph with colour for gradient and area; vocabulary: stationary, constant, decelerate. Stretch: graphs with curved sections.

lessons.unit: A13-A16 Algebra: Higher graph work and real-life graphs
lessons.title: Reciprocal and exponential graphs in real contexts
lessons.bigQuestion: When does a quantity halve as another doubles, and when does it keep multiplying?
objectives: Interpret reciprocal graphs in contexts such as shared costs
Interpret exponential growth and decay graphs and tables
Use a graph or table to solve a real problem
successCriteria: All: read values from a context graph
Most: form y = k/x and y = a × bˣ from context
Some: use trial or graph to find when a quantity crosses a value
lessons.crossCurricular: Business: shared costs; Biology and finance: growth and depreciation
lessons.smsc: Social: sharing a cost fairly between more people

keywords.def: y = k/x, a curve that falls as x rises
repeated multiplication by a factor greater than 1
repeated multiplication by a factor between 0 and 1
a line a curve approaches but never reaches

teach.heading: Reciprocal relationships
bullets: A coach costs £600, shared by n people
The more people, the smaller the share, but never zero
teach.note: Discuss fairness in sharing. Compare with y = k/x: graph never touches the axes.

model.problem: A coach costs £600 shared equally. Find C for n = 12, and how many people for C = £25.

teach.heading: Exponential growth and decay
bullets: Decay: the value falls by 15% a year
teach.note: Value of an item falls by multiplying by 0.85 each year. Depreciation is used here rather than interest-based contexts.

teach.heading: When does it cross a value?
bullets: During the fifth year the value falls below £6000
teach.note: Use a table of trial values or read the graph at £6000.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Exponential change is not linear: equal multiplications, not equal additions

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: A population is P = 200 × 3ᵗ. What is P when t = 2?

practice: Coach cost £600 shared by 12, then 20 people. Find each share.
Find N = 500 × 2ᵗ for t = 0 to 4 and plot the points
A car is worth £12 000 and loses 15% a year. Find its value after 3 years.
When does the car's value first fall below £6000?
independent: Core: (a) y = 12/x, find y when x = 3 and when x = 8 (b) 2ᵗ values for t = 0 to 5
Extend: Bacteria numbers: 800 at t = 0 and 1600 at t = 1. Find the formula and when 10 000 is first exceeded.
Stretch: Two plans: A, £40 fixed; B costs £600/n per person for n people. Find n where B is cheaper than £40.
exit: Share £480 between 8 people
N = 100 × 2ᵗ when t = 4
State the asymptote of y = 1/x.
lessons.homework: Six real-life questions: two reciprocal, two exponential growth, two decay, each with a sentence interpreting the graph.
lessons.send: Higher only. SEND/EAL: table of values scaffold; sentence frame 'every hour the number ___'. Stretch: fitting y = a × bˣ to two points.

lessons.unit: A13-A16 Algebra: Higher graph work and real-life graphs
lessons.title: Gradients of curves and rates of change
lessons.bigQuestion: How fast is something changing at one exact moment?
objectives: Estimate the gradient of a curve at a point by drawing a tangent
Estimate a gradient using chords that get closer to a point
Interpret the gradient of a curve as a rate of change
successCriteria: All: draw a tangent and read its gradient (Higher only)
Most: use chords to estimate the gradient at a point
Some: interpret the gradient with units in context
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: instantaneous speed; Biology: growth rates
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: patient refinement of an estimate towards the truth

keywords.def: a straight line that touches a curve at one point
a straight line joining two points on a curve
how quickly one quantity changes with another
at one exact moment

starter: Bismillah. Find the gradient between (3, 9) and (4, 16).

teach.heading: Tangents
bullets: Place a ruler so it touches the curve at one point
The line should not cross the curve there
Choose two far-apart points on the tangent
Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x
teach.note: On y = t², the tangent at t = 3 passes through (2, 3) and (4, 15): gradient 12 ÷ 2 = 6. Say: the speed at t = 3 is about 6 m/s.

model.problem: Estimate the gradient of s = t² at t = 3 using chords from (3, 9)

teach.heading: Chords approach the tangent
bullets: As the second point moves closer, the chord looks like the tangent
This is the idea behind differentiation
teach.note: Show the picture with a graphing tool.

teach.heading: Rates of change
bullets: Gradient units: y unit per x unit
Population against days: people per day
A steeper tangent means a faster rate
teach.note: Interpret in a sentence: 'At t = 3 s the distance is increasing at about 6 m per second.'

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: A tangent touches the curve; it should not cut through it
teach.note: Check the ruler's angle.

misconception.wrong: The gradient of a curve at a point is the gradient between the point and the origin
misconception.right: Draw the tangent at that point and use two points on the tangent

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: A tangent to a distance-time curve passes through (2, 4) and (6, 16). What does the tangent's gradient represent?
options: 3 m/s, the speed at that moment

practice: Estimate the gradient of y = x² at x = 2 using chords to x = 3, 2.5 and 2.1
Draw a tangent to y = x² at x = 1.5 and find its gradient
The tangent to a curve at t = 4 passes through (2, 5) and (6, 25). State the gradient and units.
Explain why chords give an estimate, not an exact value.
independent: Core: Use the chord method for y = x² at x = 1
Extend: From a table of s = 5t² − t at t = 2, 2.1, 2.5, 3, estimate the speed at t = 2.
Stretch: A cooling-curve tangent at 10 minutes has gradient −1.5 °C per minute. Interpret and predict the temperature change in the next 30 seconds (with a caution).
exit: What is a tangent?
Estimate the gradient from chords: 5, 4.5, 4.1 approaches ?
A tangent has gradient 8 m/s. What does it mean?
lessons.homework: Two graph-sketching tasks with tangents and one chord table; units in each answer.
lessons.send: Higher only. SEND/EAL: pre-printed curve and ruler, tangent drawn together. Stretch: gradient of y = x³ at x = 2.

lessons.unit: A13-A16 Algebra: Higher graph work and real-life graphs
lessons.title: Area under a curve and its meaning
lessons.bigQuestion: If speed is graphed against time, what does the area underneath mean?
objectives: Estimate the area under a graph using trapezia
Interpret the area under a graph in context
Decide whether an estimate is an over- or under-estimate
successCriteria: All: find areas under straight-line graphs (Higher only)
Most: estimate the area under a curve using strips
Some: interpret the area with units and judge over/under-estimate
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: distance from speed; Water supply: volume from flow rate
lessons.smsc: Social: estimating resource use responsibly (water and energy)

keywords.def: a quantity found by multiplying the y and x units
adds the areas of trapezia drawn under a curve
a vertical slice used to approximate area
an approximate answer

starter: Bismillah. Area of a trapezium with parallel sides 6 and 10 and height 2.
Area of a trapezium with sides 0 and 6, height 2.
What do you get from multiplying m/s by s?
Sketch a curve that rises quickly and then levels off.

teach.heading: Strips and trapezia
bullets: Split the area into vertical strips of equal width
Each strip: ½ × width × (left height + right height)

model.problem: A speed is measured every 2 s: 0, 6, 10, 12, 13 m/s at t = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. Estimate the distance travelled.

teach.heading: Over or under?
bullets: Chords lie below a concave curve
teach.note: Explain with a sketch.

teach.heading: Meaning of area
bullets: Area of flow rate (litres/min) against minutes: litres
Area of £ per hour against hours: £
teach.note: Flow readings 4, 6, 5 l/min at t = 0, 5, 10: area = ½·5(4 + 6) + ½·5(6 + 5) = 52.5 litres.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Use the height as the trapezium's width
teach.note: The width is along the x-axis.

misconception.wrong: Area of the strip = (y₁ + y₂) × width
misconception.right: Area of the strip = ½ × width × (y₁ + y₂)

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: Speed readings are 0 and 8 m/s at t = 0 and t = 2 s. The area of the trapezium is:

practice: Estimate the area under the curve for the readings 0, 6, 10, 12, 13 at 2-second intervals
Flow rates of 4, 6, 5 l/min at 0, 5, 10 minutes. Estimate the litres.
Explain whether the first estimate is an over- or under-estimate
What is represented by the area under a graph of £ per hour against hours?
independent: Core: Find the area under the line through (0, 2) and (6, 8), between t = 0 and 6.
Extend: Using trapezia, estimate the area under a curve with heights 2, 5, 7, 8 at x = 0, 1, 2, 3.
Stretch: Estimate with 3 strips and 6 strips for a curve with heights 0, 4, 6, 7, 7.5, 7.8, 8 at 0 to 6 and compare.
exit: Area of trapezium: parallel sides 5 and 9, height 2
What does the area under a speed-time graph represent?
Is the trapezium estimate for a rising, flattening curve too big or too small?
lessons.homework: Two estimates with trapezia, one with units and an over/under comment.
lessons.send: Higher only. SEND/EAL: pre-drawn strips on the graph; formula card for trapezium. Stretch: error reduction with narrower strips.

lessons.unit: A13-A16 Algebra: Higher graph work and real-life graphs
lessons.title: The equation of a circle and tangents to a circle
lessons.bigQuestion: How does Pythagoras describe every point on a circle?
objectives: Write the equation of a circle with centre the origin
Test whether a point lies on a circle
Find the equation of a tangent to a circle at a given point
successCriteria: All: recall x² + y² = r² (Higher only)
Most: test points and find r
Some: find the equation of a tangent using perpendicular gradients
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: circular motion; Design: circular plans

lessons.unit: A19-A20 Algebra: simultaneous equations and iteration
lessons.title: Simultaneous equations by graphs
lessons.bigQuestion: What does it mean when two lines cross?
objectives: Solve two linear simultaneous equations by drawing graphs
Check the solution in both equations
Identify when there is no solution
successCriteria: All: read the intersection point of two graphs
Most: draw both lines accurately and state the solution
Some: use graphs to estimate then confirm algebraically, and explain parallel lines
lessons.crossCurricular: Business: break-even points; Science: meeting points of two moving objects
lessons.smsc: Moral: checking solutions is part of careful work

keywords.def: two equations true at the same time
the point where two graphs cross
the pair of values satisfying both equations
never cross; same gradient

starter: Bismillah. Find y when x = 3 for y = 2x − 1.
Find y when x = 3 for x + y = 8.
Rearrange x + y = 8 to make y the subject.

teach.heading: Intersection = solution
bullets: Each point on a line satisfies its equation
y = 2x − 1 and x + y = 8 cross at (3, 5)
teach.note: Linear equations by algebra are taught in the school's Year 11 'Simultaneous linear equations' lessons; here pupils see the geometry.

model.problem: Solve y = 2x − 1 and x + y = 8 using graphs

teach.heading: Estimating then checking

teach.note: The coordinates (3, 5) mean x = 3, y = 5.

lessons.unit: A19-A20 Algebra: simultaneous equations and iteration
lessons.title: Iteration: using formulae to approximate solutions
lessons.bigQuestion: Can repeating a simple calculation lead you to the solution of an equation you cannot solve exactly?
objectives: Rearrange an equation into the form x = g(x)
Use xₙ₊₁ = g(xₙ) repeatedly with a calculator
Recognise when an iteration converges and when it does not
successCriteria: All: use xₙ₊₁ = g(xₙ) to find the next terms (Higher only)
Most: rearrange an equation to form an iteration formula
Some: compare two rearrangements and explain which converges
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: loops and algorithms; Science: numerical methods
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: perseverance, getting closer with each repetition

keywords.def: repeating a process to approach a solution
xₙ₊₁ = g(xₙ)
get closer to a value
the calculator's key for the previous answer

starter: Rearrange x³ + x − 3 = 0 to make x³ the subject.

teach.heading: The idea
bullets: x³ + x − 3 = 0 cannot be solved by factorising
Rearrange: x³ = 3 − x, so x = ∛(3 − x)
teach.note: Demonstrate using the Ans key: type 1 then ∛(3 − Ans) and press equals repeatedly.

teach.heading: Does it always work?
teach.note: Not every rearrangement converges. Pupils try both with a calculator.

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Use the previous answer, not the starting value, each time
teach.note: Show x₂ using x₁, not x₀.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: xₙ₊₁ = ∛(3 − xₙ) and x₁ = 1.2599. What is x₂ to 4 d.p.?
check.why: 3 − 1.2599 = 1.7401, and ∛1.7401 = 1.2028. D forgets the cube root.

practice: Use xₙ₊₁ = ∛(3 − xₙ) with x₀ = 1 to find x₁, x₂, x₃
Show that x³ + x − 3 = 0 can be written x = ∛(3 − x)
Try xₙ₊₁ = 3 − xₙ³ from x₀ = 1 and describe what happens
Show that x³ + 2x − 5 = 0 can be rearranged to x = ∛(5 − 2x)
independent: Core: xₙ₊₁ = √(2xₙ + 3), x₀ = 2: find x₁ to x₄
Extend: For x³ + 2x − 5 = 0 use xₙ₊₁ = ∛(5 − 2xₙ) from x₀ = 1.3 to find a solution to 3 d.p.
Stretch: For x² − x − 1 = 0, try xₙ₊₁ = 1 + 1/xₙ and xₙ₊₁ = xₙ² − 1; find which converges from x₀ = 1.5, and explain.
exit: Rearrange x³ = 7 − 2x to x = ∛(7 − 2x)
x₀ = 2, xₙ₊₁ = √(xₙ + 6). Find x₁ and x₂.
Do repeated values that settle near one number show convergence?
lessons.homework: Four iteration tasks on the calculator, one with a divergent rearrangement; record each xₙ.
lessons.send: Higher only. SEND/EAL: Ans-key step cards; table template for n and xₙ. Stretch: staircase and cobweb diagrams.

lessons.unit: A19-A20 Algebra: simultaneous equations and iteration
lessons.title: Locating roots: sign change and decimal search
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you be certain that a solution lies in a particular interval?
objectives: Show a root lies in an interval using a change of sign
Narrow an interval by decimal search
Give a root to a required accuracy and justify it
successCriteria: All: evaluate f(x) at two values and compare signs (Higher only)
Most: use a change of sign to show a root lies between two values
Some: prove a root to 2 decimal places using bounds on f
lessons.smsc: Moral: proving a claim rather than asserting it

keywords.def: f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs
a value where f(x) = 0
an unbroken graph with no jumps
testing smaller intervals

starter: Bismillah. Evaluate x³ + x − 3 at x = 1 and x = 2.

teach.heading: Sign change means a root
bullets: Opposite signs: a root lies between 1 and 2
The graph is continuous so it must cross y = 0
teach.note: State both conditions: change of sign and continuous. Pupils write this as a sentence.

model.problem: Show x³ + x − 3 = 0 has a root between 1.2 and 1.25

teach.heading: Proving to 2 d.p.
bullets: Change of sign: root is in (1.205, 1.215), so root = 1.21 to 2 d.p.
teach.note: Use the calculator's table or Ans. This is how an exam asks 'show that the root is 1.21 to 2 d.p.'

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: The values must be tested with a sign, not just 'close to zero'
teach.note: Close to zero is not enough.

misconception.wrong: f(1.2) = −0.072 is close to 0 so x = 1.2 is the root
misconception.right: The sign change between 1.2 and 1.25 shows the root lies between them

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Whiteboards.

check.q: f(1.3) = −0.2 and f(1.4) = 0.5. What can you say?
check.why: The sign change in a continuous function shows a root lies between 1.3 and 1.4. A needs more evidence.

practice: Show that x³ + 2x − 5 = 0 has a root between 1 and 2
Show that the root is between 1.3 and 1.4
Show x³ + x − 3 = 0 has root 1.21 to 2 d.p.
State why f needs to be continuous
independent: Core: f(x) = x³ − 4x − 1: find f(2) and f(3) and state what you can say; then f(2.1), f(2.2).
Extend: For x³ + 2x − 5 = 0 use xₙ₊₁ = ∛(5 − 2xₙ) from x₀ = 1.3, then prove the root to 2 d.p.
Stretch: Explain why f(x) = 1/x has f(−1) < 0 < f(1) but no root between −1 and 1.
exit: Show x³ − 3x + 1 = 0 has a root between 1 and 2 (f(1) = −1, f(2) = 3)
What does a change of sign show?
What must be true of f for the change-of-sign argument to work?
lessons.homework: Three 'show that a root lies between' questions and one iteration then bounds proof.
lessons.send: Higher only. SEND/EAL: template 'f(a) = __, f(b) = __, signs differ, so root between a and b'. Stretch: bisection to 3 d.p.
